content_metadata.description: An overview of different types of galaxies, their classification, evolution, and interactions in the universe.

qAndA.answer: Spiral galaxies have a prominent disk structure with spiral arms, whereas elliptical galaxies are smooth and featureless.
qAndA.question: What distinguishes a spiral galaxy from an elliptical galaxy?

qAndA.answer: Galaxies can interact through tidal forces, which arise due to their close proximity and gravitational pull.
qAndA.question: How can galaxies interact with each other?

qAndA.answer: There are estimated to be around 10 to the power of 11 galaxies in the observable universe.
qAndA.question: What is the estimated number of galaxies in the universe?

qAndA.answer: The Hubble Tuning Fork Diagram provides a classification scheme for galaxies based on their morphology, enabling astronomers to study and understand galaxy populations.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the Hubble Tuning Fork Diagram?

qAndA.answer: While we can't see the full view of the Milky Way from Earth, parts of its spiral arms are visible to us as a band of stars across the night sky.
qAndA.question: How can we observe the spiral structure of our own galaxy, the Milky Way?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: A galaxy can be roughly defined as a collection of stars, gas and dust and they are all
gravitational bound as a single entity.
These galaxies are the building blocks of our universe.
In reality, we encounter a wide variety of galaxies.
Some of them are elliptical in shape and are rather feature less.
They are called the elliptical galaxies like the NGC 4150 galaxies shown here in the right.
There are other galaxies too, which have a dysmorphology and often exhibit spectacular spiral
structure.
The world pool galaxy is a classic example of this kind of galaxies which is shown in the
left.
These are called dys galaxies.
Since they have the spiral structure, often they are alternately referred as spiral
galaxies.
Now, to understand the population of galaxies in a better note, one needs to classify
them based on some common characteristics they share.
It was the great astronomer Edwin P. Hubble who first classified the morphology of galaxies
in the local universe.
The resulting classification scheme is popularly known as the Hubble Tuning Fog diagram.
As the classification scheme, we are close resemblance with the tuning for structure,
which is shown here.
On the left, we have the elliptical galaxies and on the right, we have the dys galaxies.
The current understanding is that our dys galaxy grows in size by marching with other galaxies
and at the end, they become the ellipticals.
Now our galaxy, the Milky Way, which hosts the solar system is also a dys galaxy, which
has spiral arms.
It can contain around 10 to the power 11 stars in it.
Since we are residing within it, therefore you cannot see the full view and the picture
shown on the left is merely an artist impression.
Nevertheless, some part of the spiral arms of the Milky Way is feasible to us.
There is a picture showing a part of the spiral structure.
This picture is taken from the from from 80s, Neu Nithal India.
Finally, there are estimated to be around 10 to the power 11 galaxies in the universe.
Often they come very close to each other and therefore they pull or interact tidally.
In the extreme case, one galaxy can get trapped into the gravitational potential of the
other galaxy as a result.
Finally, they march with each other.
Here are some of the real images of the galaxy interactions where the galaxies are caught
in the action.
These images are taken from the European Southern Observatory's website.
